title: AI Agents Now Take Entire Online College Courses for Students
excerpt: Autonomous AI tools log into course management platforms like Canvas and complete assignments, quizzes, and exams without student involvement, prompting universities to abandon detection software and redesign assessments.
body:
• Autonomous AI agents can log into platforms like Canvas and complete entire online courses — including assignments, quizzes, and exams — without student involvement.
  • At least 9% of college students who use generative AI report using it to cheat, according to a 95,000-student study published in Science.
  • Universities including Yale, Northwestern, and Georgetown are abandoning AI detectors due to unreliability and shifting toward assessment redesign.

The AI cheating crisis in higher education has entered a new phase. Autonomous AI agents — software that can browse the web, log into accounts, and take independent actions — are now being used to complete entire online college courses, from discussion posts to final exams, without the enrolled student lifting a finger.

The tools work by connecting directly to learning management systems like Canvas, reading assignments, generating responses, and submitting them. Some products go further, tracking deadlines, participating in forums, and even adapting their writing style to mimic a particular student's voice. The result is a fully automated path to a degree that bypasses the educational process entirely.

The Scale of the Problem

A landmark study of more than 95,000 undergraduates at 20 research-intensive U.S. universities, published in Science in May 2026, found that about two-thirds of students use generative AI and nearly 40% use it at least monthly. At least 9% of AI-using students admitted to using it to cheat — a figure researchers at UC Berkeley, Cornell, and the University of Technology Sydney called "very serious."

https://x.com/DigitalTrends/status/2088049678575448329

"Even this early stage evidence shows that we have a very serious challenge on our hands, and universities need to address that."

— Igor Chirikov, UC Berkeley researcher

The problem extends well beyond chatbot-assisted essays. Faculty at Brown University let students take home an exam where the average score is typically 65 to 80 percent. Students scored an average of 96 percent. When the same class took a final exam under controlled conditions, the average plummeted to a record-low 48.6 percent.

Why Detection Is Failing

Universities are increasingly conceding that AI detection tools do not work. Studies have shown that detectors from companies including OpenAI, GPTZero, and Copyleaks exhibit inconsistencies, produce false positives when evaluating human-written work, and are biased against non-native English speakers. Some false accusations have led to student lawsuits against universities.

At least a dozen institutions — including Yale, Northwestern, Georgetown, and Indiana University — have either banned faculty reliance on AI detectors as sole evidence of cheating or disabled Turnitin's AI detection feature entirely. Indiana's Kelley School of Business now tells faculty: "Instead of trying to 'catch' AI use, focus on designing assignments that encourage process, reasoning, and authentic engagement."

Students are also deploying counter-tools. "Humanizer" programs rewrite AI-generated text to evade detection, while "autotypers" simulate the uneven pace of human typing, complete with fake deletions and backspacing. TikTok and YouTube tutorials walk students through the entire process step by step.

The Redesign Response

Faced with an arms race they cannot win, faculty are reluctantly overhauling their assessments. Options range from oral examinations and blue-book in-class essays to assignments that require students to document their reasoning process rather than simply submit a finished product.

"We cannot be giving unsupervised assessments to students expecting them to resist AI. They're not going to be learning, we're going to be spending our time trying to catch them cheating."

— Tricia Bertram Gallant, UC San Diego academic integrity director

But the redesign effort faces significant practical constraints. Oral exams and supervised writing require far more faculty time and cannot easily scale to large lecture courses with hundreds of students. Marc Watkins, director of the AI Institute for Teachers at the University of Mississippi, said he "can't even fathom the cost" for a single university to undertake the transition.

What Comes Next

The technology shows no signs of slowing. A Notre Dame freshman recently built an AI agent called Kerra that connects to Canvas, reads assignments and grades, generates study guides and assignment drafts, and sends deadline reminders via text. More than 1,000 students signed up within an hour before the university shut it down and launched an investigation.

As AI agents grow more capable and accessible, the gap between what students are expected to learn and what they actually demonstrate will continue to widen — unless institutions fundamentally rethink how they measure learning in the age of artificial intelligence.
